## 1. System context and trust boundaries

### 1.1 Components

```
 ┌────────────────────────── user session (uid = 501) ────────────────────────────┐
 │  LockPlus.app (hardened runtime, NOT sandboxed, Developer ID in Release)         │
 │   SwiftUI windows · MenuBarController · ProfileStore · CredentialStore(app)     │
 │   Sparkle 2.10.1 · SystemExtensionManager · TunnelServiceClient (XPC)           │
 │   ~/Library/Application Support/io.github.steiale.lockplus.mac/  (0700)          │
 │   Data-protection keychain, group M53GHX9FAY.io.github.steiale.lockplus.mac     │
 │   XPCServices/LockPlusValidator.xpc: profile checks (sandboxed, user; 2.0.2)    │
 └───────────────┬─────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
       NETunnelProviderManager API         NSXPCConnection(machServiceName: …tunnel.vN,
       (start/stop, NEVPNStatus,           options: .privileged), both ends pin code signature
       fetchLastDisconnectError)                │
 ┌───────────────▼──────────────┐   ┌──────────▼─────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ nesessionmanager / NE prefs  │──▶│ LockPlusTunnel.systemextension (root, sandboxed) │
 │ (system-wide VPN configs,    │   │  PacketTunnelProvider → TunnelController (actor) │
 │  on-demand evaluation)       │   │  WireGuardAdapter → libwg-go (WireGuardKitGo     │
 └──────────────────────────────┘   │    fork patches, wireguard-go master)            │
                                    │  OpenVPNAdapterImpl → OpenVPN3Shim (openvpn3     │
                                    │    release/3.11.8 + OpenSSL 3.5 LTS, static)     │
                                    │  TunnelServiceListener (XPC, process scope)      │
                                    │  ExtensionSecretStore: System keychain (primary) │
                                    │    or sealed root 0600 container files (S4)      │
                                    └──────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                                               │ UDP/TCP to VPN servers (bypasses tunnel)
                                       ┌───────▼────────┐
                                       │ Internet / LAN │  VPN servers, DNS, appcast host
                                       └────────────────┘
 Sparkle: appcast (GitHub Pages, HTTPS, signed feed) + archives (GitHub Releases, EdDSA)
```

### 1.2 Trust boundaries

| # | Boundary | Crossing data | Who must distrust whom |
|---|---|---|---|
| B1 | App ↔ extension (XPC) | profile payloads, credentials, auth answers, status/stats (draft 8: no logs, §5.2) | **The extension distrusts the app's input**: it re-validates every payload (§8.1; 2.0.2: memory-safe Swift checks at provision, plus openvpn3's parser differential at start). Both verify the peer's code signature (§5.3). Several app instances (other users, fast user switching) may be connected at once; events are filtered by owner uid (§5.2). |
| B2 | App/ext ↔ NE preferences | non-secret profile config | Readable by any local admin and visible in System Settings, so it holds no secrets (§3.3). |
| B3 | User ↔ app (files, zip, clipboard; 2.0.2: also files opened from Finder or the Dock, §11.1) | untrusted profiles | Every parser treats its input as hostile, with caps (§3.5, §8.1, §9.1). |
| B4 | Extension ↔ VPN server | handshake, pushed options, packets | A server can be malicious or MITM'd. Pushed options are allowlisted (§8.5). |
| B5 | App ↔ update channel | appcast, archives | The EdDSA key is the trust anchor (Sparkle accepts a changed code-signing identity when EdDSA validates). Signed feed, no automatic downgrades (§12). |
| B6 | Extension ↔ its secret store | secrets at rest | Root is the boundary: the System keychain (primary) and the sealed root-owned 0600 container files (fallback) are both readable by root and by nobody else. Any admin can become root, so admins are out of scope (§6.3). |
| B7 | App ↔ legacy Go app | tunnel files, legacy keychain, helper socket | Read-only and copy-only. Legacy data is validated like any import (§13). |
| B8 | App ↔ validator service (2.0.2, XPC) | untrusted profile and zip bytes in; fixed-shape verdicts and entries out | **Both distrust each other.** The service is sandboxed with no network, files or keychain and parses only what it is sent (§2.4, §8.1); it accepts only `APP_REQ` peers. The app pins `VALIDATOR_REQ` and treats every reply as untrusted data (caps before decode, `isWireValid`, names never become paths; §5.3). A compromised service can lie about a verdict, but the extension re-runs [1]–[5] and the fixed point at provision and [6] at start, and the session's own connect runs [7]. |

### 1.3 Threat model (STRIDE per adversary)

**A1. Local malware running as the same user (no root, no TCC grants).**
- *Spoofing:* it connects to our Mach service and pretends to be the app.
  - Mitigation: the listener sets `setConnectionCodeSigningRequirement` (§5.3), so an unsigned or foreign-team peer is rejected on its first message, before the delegate or any handler runs.
- *Spoofing the extension to the app:* it registers a lookalike listener so the app's first message reaches it.
  - Mitigation: the app connects with `.privileged`, so only a root-registered (global bootstrap) name matches; `hello` carries nothing secret, and no secret-bearing call is sent before `hello`'s reply has passed `EXT_REQ` on that connection (§5.3; ref/xpc-servicemanagement §0 fact 2).
- *Tampering:* it modifies `/Applications/LockPlus.app`, which a drag-install leaves user-writable.
  - Mitigation: a modified bundle fails dynamic code validation, so the extension refuses it, and the hardened runtime blocks DYLD injection. A modified app also loses its restricted, profile-authorised `keychain-access-groups` entitlement, so it cannot read the data-protection items of our group and cannot unseal anything (§2.4; the team-prefixed app group is **not** a keychain access group and nothing relies on it, ref/security C7). §15.6 tests this with a tampered copy of the real app.
  - **Decision:** no launch constraints in v2.0 (draft 1 claimed they re-check; none were configured). Gatekeeper only assesses quarantined first launches, so it is not counted as a control here. Launch/environment constraints are listed under Later (§21).
- *Tampering:* it rewrites `profiles/*.json` metadata, hoping the app faithfully re-saves a weakened policy (e.g. `killSwitch = false`) to NE preferences on the next reconcile.
  - Mitigation: each metadata file carries an HMAC-SHA256 over its canonical JSON, keyed by a subkey derived from the master sealing key (§3.3, §3.4). Same-user code cannot read that key, so it cannot forge the HMAC. A mismatch quarantines the file and never propagates to NE preferences.
  - Replaying an older, validly MAC'd file is caught by the `metaRevision` counter inside the MAC, compared against the NE manager's `metaRev` before any re-save (§3.4, N6).
  - The extension takes policy only from NE preferences (written through `nesessionmanager`, not a user-writable file) and from its own provisioned copy.
- *Information disclosure:* it reads App Support.
  - Mitigation: payloads are AES-GCM-sealed with a key in the data-protection keychain (§3.4). Same-user code without our team signature cannot read that key.
  - Credentials live only in the keychains.
  - **This is an improvement over the Go app, which kept plaintext 0600 files.**
- *Information disclosure:* it reads unified logs.
  - Mitigation: secrets never reach `Logger` (§14). Dynamic strings are `.private`.
- *Denial of service:* it runs `scutil --nc stop`, kills the app, or floods XPC.
  - Accepted, because same-user code can always disrupt.
  - Kill-switch profiles fail closed while reasserting, held, and while a start is pending (S2 E4, E14a; draft 9). A user stop (`scutil --nc stop`) opens, as designed; a killed provider opens for ~2.5 s until NE restarts it (S2 E1, §10.1.1, §20 risk 24).
  - The XPC listener enforces size caps, post-decode range checks, per-handler deadlines and (draft 8) at most 8 in-flight handlers per connection (§5.2, §5.4). There is no per-connection rate limiting in v2.0 (§21): same-user code can flood XPC anyway, and that only costs it CPU.
- *Elevation of privilege:* it uses the root extension as a confused deputy (file read/write, exec).
  - Mitigation: the extension is sandboxed and exposes no path-taking or exec-taking API.
  - Profiles go through an allowlist with no path directives (§8.1), and openvpn3 has no script hooks.
  - *2.0.2:* no extension method runs openvpn3 or OpenSSL on bytes a caller sends; that happens only in the sandboxed validator service (B8, §8.1), whose name only the containing app can look up and whose listener requires `APP_REQ`.
- *Starting our profiles (2.0.2, D10.4-5):* `scutil --nc start` (or a System Settings toggle) of a profile without Auto-Connect is refused with 225 (§7.2). It can't arm a start: `armStart` needs an `APP_REQ` peer. It can still start an Auto-Connect profile (the owner opted into unattended starts) and stop any session (the denial of service accepted above).

**A2. Other local users.**
- NE configurations are system-wide, so another user can see the profile names in System Settings and try to start them. *2.0.2 (D10.4-5):* only starts the owner authorised are honoured (§7.2); another user can start only the owner's Auto-Connect profiles.
- *Disclosure:* a non-admin user cannot read the payload or credentials. App Support is 0700, the data-protection keychain is per-user, and the extension's store (System keychain items or root 0600 files) is root-only (§6.3).
- **Out of scope: admin users.** An admin can become root and read the extension's store, the extension's memory, and anything else root can. Root is the real boundary of the extension store whichever S4 variant wins; no keychain ACL changes that (an admin can also read System keychain items). This is stated in the user docs.
- *Tampering:* another user's copy of LockPlus sees our managers through `loadAllFromPreferences` (S2 E13 on 26, draft 9: status and flags visible, although Apple documents only "configurations created by the calling app"; ref/networkextension C29). The checks below hold either way.
  - Mitigation: `providerConfiguration.ownerUID`. The app hides and refuses to edit foreign profiles.
  - The extension enforces ownership on every profile-scoped XPC call using the peer's `effectiveUserIdentifier` (§5.4).
  - **The extension store is namespaced by uid (draft 8, D8-1, §6.3).** Every secret is addressed by (ownerUID, kind, UUID), so another user who learns a profile UUID (NE preferences are world-readable) can't squat it: provisioning that UUID creates B's own entry and leaves A's untouched. Before draft 8 the first uid to provision a UUID owned it, which allowed a provision DoS and, worse, A's start loading B's payload (Fable review H1).
  - **`providerConfiguration.ownerUID` is app-asserted (draft 8, D8-2, PF 47).** The app that saves the NE configuration writes it, and nothing in NE binds it to the saving user. The extension looks the payload up in that uid's namespace, so `runStarting`'s `entry.ownerUID == cfg.ownerUID` check holds by construction: it is a consistency check, not a boundary.
  - **S2 E13 (draft 9, D9-13): another local user can start and stop our configurations.** Another user's LockPlus (or System Settings, or `scutil --nc`) can start our manager from `.disconnected`, which connects **our** provisioned profile with **our** stored credentials, and can stop a session we started; the extension accepted that user's XPC `hello` (`peerUID` differs). It still cannot read the payload or the credentials (uid-namespaced store, root-only), receive our prompts, events or snapshots (uid filtering, below), or change the payload (provisioning writes only its own uid's namespace). **Accepted residual for v2.0** (lead decision, §20 risk 23): no provider-side start control (the start's audit token or a per-uid start capability) and no "connected by another user" UI. Revisit if multi-user Macs show up in the field. *Superseded for starts in 2.0.2 (below); stops are unchanged.*
  - **Start authorisation (2.0.2, D10.4-5, §7.2).** The extension honours a start of a profile only when (a) it carries the nonce of an arm made over XPC within 15 s by a connection whose kernel-reported uid is the profile's `ownerUID` and that has the profile provisioned in its own namespace, (b) it is NE's replay of a session so authorised (same nonce), or (c) it is unattended (no `lp.manual`) and the profile has on-demand rules (the owner turned on Auto-Connect). Anything else is refused with `.startNotAuthorised` (225) before any payload or credential read and without touching a running session. So another local user can no longer connect our manual profiles with our stored credentials, from System Settings, `scutil` or their own LockPlus, and can't route their traffic through our authenticated tunnel by starting it. **What it does not cover (accepted, plan §S.4):** (a) our Auto-Connect profiles can still be started by anyone (D-1: the owner opted into unattended starts); (b) stops can't be authorised (NE gives the provider no initiator for `stopTunnel`), so another user can still stop our session; (c) while our tunnel is up, every user's traffic uses it (macOS VPNs are system-wide); (d) another user's armed kill-switch start of **their own** profile still ends our split session, visibly (223, D-2).
- *Disclosure through events:* another user's validly signed LockPlus passes `APP_REQ`, so the signature check is no help here. **uid filtering is the only control:** profile-scoped `tunnelEvent`s, auth prompts and snapshots go only to connections whose uid equals the profile's `ownerUID`; other connections get a content-free "a LockPlus tunnel changed state" event (§5.2; ref/xpc-servicemanagement C7). *Draft 8 (Fable M1, M2):* a `tunnelSnapshot` for a profile that isn't the running session discloses nothing about that session (§5.2), and the log methods that let any uid read engine lines are gone.
- *Residual risk:* another user can stop a tunnel from System Settings, `scutil --nc` or their own copy of LockPlus, and start our Auto-Connect profiles (S2 E13; 2.0.2 refuses their starts of our other profiles). This is documented and inherent to macOS.
- *Start guard policy (draft 10.3, §7.2, §20 risk 27):* with two configurations started at once, the extension runs one session. A kill-switch start wins over a session without the kill switch (that session is ended visibly); otherwise the first session wins and the other start fails. Another local user can therefore keep one of our split profiles from starting by running a session of their own or of one of our Auto-Connect profiles (2.0.2: no longer of our manual profiles; denial of service, closed for kill-switch profiles), and can end a running split session by an armed start of a kill-switch profile of their own (D-2).

**A3. Malicious profiles (.ovpn/.conf/zip from an attacker; 2.0.2: also opened from Finder or the Dock).**
- Root file read/write, library loading and exec through directives.
  - Mitigation: an allowlist, the openvpn-exact tokenizer, and a canonical re-serialization verified by openvpn3's own parser and by constructing openvpn3's `ClientOptions` (§8.1; 2.0.2: both in the sandboxed validator service).
  - The extension re-validates the profile (2.0.2: [1]–[5] and the canonical fixed point at provision, + [6] at start) and runs sandboxed. openvpn3 is built with `USE_TUN_BUILDER` only, so no code path can shell out to `route`/`ifconfig` (§8.1).
- Parser memory-safety bugs in openvpn3's C++.
  - Mitigation: fuzzing with ASan on macOS (§15.4; draft 8: Xcode 27.1 has no libFuzzer for Swift, so the targets run under an ASan + coverage mutation driver).
  - The extension parses only canonical text it generated itself after validation.
  - *2.0.2 (D10.4-1):* attacker-chosen bytes reach openvpn3's C++ and OpenSSL's PEM/ASN.1 parsers only in the validator service: sandboxed, no network, no files, running as the user, a 10 s watchdog, one request at a time. Root runs openvpn3 only on a stored canonical payload: its `OptionList` at start ([6]) and the session's own connect ([7]). Before 2.0.2, `validateProfile` let any validly signed peer of any uid feed [7] in root.
- Zip bombs and zip-slip.
  - Mitigation: 500 entries max, 1 MiB per entry decompressed (2.0.2; was 10 MiB), 64 MiB unpacked in total (2.0.2; was 100 MiB), 1 MiB per raw profile (256 KiB canonical, §8.1), and nothing is unpacked to disk. *2.0.2:* the archive is read in the validator service; the app gets fixed-shape entries and issues (§3.5).
- Images (QR).
  - QR import does not exist (2.0.2, D-3: the dead entry points are removed); a dropped image file (`.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.heic`, by name) is refused as "Images aren't supported." and never decoded; any other file goes through the profile pipeline. A later QR decoder runs inside the validator service (§21).
- Display-name injection.
  - Mitigation: names never touch a path (UUID keys) and are validated (§3.1).
- An export-time injection into wg-quick (newline in a value).
  - Mitigation: the validator rejects `\r`/`\n` in every value, a port of `internal/config/validator.go`.

**A4. Malicious or MITM VPN server.**
- *Spoofing:* a WireGuard peer is authenticated by its key.
  - OpenVPN uses `remote-cert-tls`/`verify-x509-name` from the profile. **Decision:** if a profile has neither `remote-cert-tls server` nor `verify-x509-name`/`peer-fingerprint`, import warns with "server identity not pinned" (not fatal, for compatibility).
  - **openvpn3 before `release/3.11.8` (and master as of 2026-10-17) silently ignores a profile's `remote-cert-tls`** (ref/openvpn3 §1 item 3). We pin `release/3.11.8` (O2). Defence in depth: when the canonical profile has `remote-cert-tls server` and no explicit `remote-cert-eku`, the normalizer appends `remote-cert-eku "TLS Web Server Authentication"`, which every version enforces. Regression test LK-OVPN-CERT (§15.2): a server presenting a CA-signed certificate **without** the server EKU must fail with `CERT_VERIFY_FAIL` when the profile has `remote-cert-tls server`, and also when only the appended `remote-cert-eku` is present; it re-runs on every openvpn3 bump. S13 confirmed both on 3.11.8. A certificate with only the clientAuth EKU does not discriminate: OpenSSL's default TLS-client purpose check rejects it even without `remote-cert-tls` (draft 7).
- *Tampering* through pushed options:
  - routes are clamped (§8.5); `redirect-gateway` changes no local policy;
  - DNS is applied only through `NEDNSSettings`;
  - nothing pushed can execute anything;
  - `auth-token` is stored in memory only, never logged.
- *Disclosure:* a hostile LAN or server steers traffic around the tunnel (TunnelVision CVE-2024-3661, TunnelCrack LocalNet and ServerIP).
  - With the kill switch on, `includeAllNetworks` defeats DHCP option 121 (TunnelVision).
  - **Decision:** `excludeLocalNetworks` ("Allow LAN") defaults to **off** for every profile (LocalNet attack) and is a visible per-profile toggle. UI-CONCEPT shows it off (F-1).
  - ServerIP: no excluded host route to the server is ever installed (§8.5, Conflicts d), so a spoofed server address cannot pull other processes' traffic out of the tunnel. LK-16 tests it.
  - **Residuals, documented (§10.1.2):** with the kill switch **off**, TunnelVision applies (a rogue DHCP server's option-121 routes are more specific than the tunnel's); split-tunnel route protection (`enforceRoutes`) scopes the tunnel's own routes but does not block other traffic.
- *Denial of service:* the server refuses or drops the connection.
  - Mitigation: capped backoff (L-RC-3). Stored credentials are never auto-retried after AUTH_FAILED (account lockout).
- *Elevation:* a memory bug in openvpn3 or wireguard-go reachable from the network.
  - Mitigations: sandboxed extension; pinned upstreams (openvpn3 `release/3.11.8`, wireguard-go master with `2631ce9`/`b3bc704`, OpenSSL 3.5 LTS); fuzzing; a monthly dependency watch plus a 14-day release SLA for upstream High/Critical fixes (§9.2, §22).

**A5. Compromised update channel.**
- Attack: a replaced appcast or archive.
  - Mitigation: an EdDSA signature on every archive with the public key in Info.plist, and `SURequireSignedFeed` (Sparkle **2.10.1** pinned exactly; floor 2.9.6 for GHSA-3x7w-j75x-ppq5 / GHSA-4v99-qgq9-6pxp, CVE-2026-47121/47122) (§12.1).
  - HTTPS only.
  - **Not a control:** Sparkle's code-signing check. Once the old EdDSA key validates the archive, Sparkle accepts **any** valid code signature on the new app, ad hoc included; it compares no team or designated requirement and never checks nested code, so it never looks at the system extension's signature (ref/sparkle §0 fact 1, C3). The EdDSA key is therefore the single trust anchor.
  - **Residual:** a signed feed has no timestamp, so whoever can write gh-pages can replay an older validly signed feed and freeze users on their current version (no downgrade, §12.1). Accepted; the served feed is verified after every publish (§12.4).
- Attack: a downgrade to a vulnerable build.
  - Mitigation: Sparkle refuses it twice: the appcast driver offers only newer `CFBundleVersion`s, and the installer aborts with `SUDowngradeError` if the host is newer (ref/sparkle §0 fact 7). There is no `bestValidUpdate` override (C4).
  - The app never submits an activation request for a lower extension version on its own; `actionForReplacingExtension` returns `.cancel` for a lower version (§4.3). The only downgrade path is the user-initiated, confirmed "Reinstall tunnel component" (§4.6).
- Attack: a stolen EdDSA key.
  - Mitigation: the key never enters CI. Archives and the appcast are signed on the dev Mac (`sign_update`/`generate_appcast` reading the key from the login keychain), with an offline backup in 1Password (§12.1).
  - **The dev Mac also builds what it signs (N1).** If CI built and notarized the archive and the dev Mac only EdDSA-signed it, a CI compromise could still get any binary signed: the dev Mac would sign whatever CI produced. CI therefore holds no Developer ID identity, no provisioning profile, no notarization key and no EdDSA key, and produces no release artifact. The release archive is built, Developer ID-signed, notarized, stapled and EdDSA-signed on the dev Mac from a clean checkout of the signed release tag (§12.4). A CI compromise can then tamper only with CI results (tests), not with anything users install.
  - **Blast-radius limits if the key is stolen anyway:** a different-team app installed this way (a) fails the extension's XPC requirement, which pins team `M53GHX9FAY` and, in Release, Developer ID (§5.3), so it cannot reach provisioned secrets; (b) cannot replace our system extension, because the system only replaces an extension with one from the same team, and an extension must be notarized to activate; (c) cannot read the app's data-protection keychain items, whose access group is a restricted entitlement authorised by our team's provisioning profile, so sealed payloads stay sealed. Notarization of the **app** is **not** claimed as a limit: Sparkle strips quarantine and never checks notarization, so Gatekeeper does not assess Sparkle-installed updates. What the attacker does get is code execution as the user (A1 capabilities) plus the user's trust in the app name. Recovery: rotate the key (below) and publish an advisory (§22).
  - **Rotation (corrects N1; ref/sparkle C2, §4.3):** with `SUVerifyUpdateBeforeExtraction = YES` (§12.1):
    - **Old key leaked but still held:** ship N+1 as a normal **zip** signed with the **old** key, carrying the new `SUPublicEDKey`; sign the feed with the old key. From N+2 on, items and feed use the new key. Sparkle's prevalidated path never checks the new key against the archive. Clients that never update stay exposed (no revocation exists).
    - **Old key lost:** ship N+1 as a Developer ID-signed (`codesign` on the `.dmg` file itself), notarized, stapled **DMG** whose `edSignature` is made with the **new** key; deltas cannot use this fallback; the `generate_appcast` folder holds only that DMG. The feed can only be signed with the new key, so clients reject it until their `SUSignedFeedFailureExpirationInterval` (20 days, set explicitly) expires and then see the item in Sparkle's safe mode (no release notes). Announce out of band.
    - Both paths are rehearsed once before GA (§15.5).

**A6. Physical access to an unlocked Mac.**
- Exporting or viewing secrets.
  - Mitigation: Reveal ("Show password", the editor's key "Show"), Edit-config, Duplicate, Export and Export-all require `LAContext` `.deviceOwnerAuthentication` (Touch ID, a paired Watch, or the login password). `RevealGate` keeps **one** evaluated `LAContext` and its own `validUntil = now + 60 s`, and calls `invalidate()` at expiry, on screen lock, on sleep and on app deactivation. `touchIDAuthenticationAllowableReuseDuration` stays 0: it only reuses a recent *device unlock*, never an in-app match (ref/security C10).
  - **Limit, stated honestly (M8 decision):** the gate is enforced by **our code**, not by the OS. The sealing key and the saved credentials are readable by the app without user presence, because provisioning and reconcile must run unattended. The gate holds against the A6 adversary only because that adversary can't run code inside our signed process: the hardened runtime blocks injection, a modified bundle loses keychain access, and same-user tools such as Terminal or `security` aren't in our access group. It does **not** hold against a bug in our app that reaches `payload(for:)` without the gate, or against an admin (A2). A unit test asserts that every UI path to plaintext goes through `RevealGate` (§15.1).
  - **Keychain Access is a second door with the same key (ref/security C12):** it lists data-protection *password* items and reveals them after the login password. Someone who knows the login password can therefore read the saved passwords (and, if stored as a password item, the sealing key) without `RevealGate`. That is the same factor `RevealGate`'s password fallback accepts, so the gate's strength is unchanged; the user docs say so. S4 checks whether the master key can be stored as a `kSecClassKey` item, which Keychain Access does not show for the DP keychain; if so, it is.
  - **Screen capture and clipboard (F-7):** secret-showing windows set `NSWindow.sharingType = .none`, copied secrets are concealed and auto-cleared, and the editor is never restored or autosaved (§11.4). These are hygiene against casual capture, not a boundary.
  - **Decision:** no separate OS-enforced reveal key in v2.0. The candidate design (an HPKE copy of each payload sealed to a Secure Enclave key with `SecAccessControl(.userPresence)`) is in §21.
- Disconnecting the VPN or disabling the kill switch.
  - Possible by design for the user. Changing the kill switch requires the tunnel to be disconnected (L-KS-2), so it is visible.
- Reading the extension's store.
  - Requires root, i.e. an admin password (out of scope, A2). In the fallback, the Secure Enclave wrap makes a copied file or disk image useless on another machine; for the System keychain no off-machine property is claimed (§3.3). On this Mac, a live root process can read either.

### 1.4 Security invariants (checked in review and in tests)

1. No secret in `providerConfiguration`, `UserDefaults`, plaintext files, logs, crash reports, XPC error strings, `NSError.userInfo`, the pasteboard beyond 60 s (§11.4), or window-restoration state.
2. The extension never trusts the app's validation. Every payload is re-validated at provision **and** at connect. *2.0.2 (D10.4-1):* the extension re-runs the memory-safe part: [1]–[5] and the canonical fixed point at provision, plus the [6] differential at start, on the session's own payload; [7] runs in the sandboxed validator service at import and inside the session's own connect. No extension method feeds a caller's bytes to openvpn3 or OpenSSL (`evaluateBytes` is allowed only under `Packages/ProfileValidator/` and `Packages/OpenVPN3Shim/`, `lint.sh`; `provision` never calls `validateForStart`, a TunnelEngine test).
3. Every XPC call has a timeout. No call waits for a tunnel connect. No secret-bearing call precedes a validated `hello` reply on the same connection (§5.3).
4. The kill-switch policy lives only in the NE configuration's protocol flags (L-LC-4); settings-level flags are never set (§10.1).
5. The extension links no AppKit, SwiftUI or Sparkle (L-EXT-5). CI greps `otool -L`.
6. The extension's secrets exist at rest only in its S4-selected store: System keychain items it created, or root-owned 0600 sealed files in its sandbox container (§6.3). Never both at once for one profile.
7. The Sparkle EdDSA private key, the Developer ID signing identity, the Developer ID provisioning profiles and the notarization credentials never exist on a CI runner. Release artifacts are built and signed only on the dev Mac (§12.1, §12.4).
8. openvpn3 is compiled with `USE_TUN_BUILDER`, and no object from `openvpn/tun/mac/client` is linked. CI checks the symbols (§8.1); the only exec-family import allowed in the extension is `_execve` attributed solely to `libwg-go.a` (draft 8, Conflicts be). (S14: holds; `openvpn/netconf/hwaddr.hpp` still inlines `tun/mac/gw.hpp`, a PF_ROUTE read for `IV_HWADDR` under `push-peer-info`, which is outside `tun/mac/client` and is noted for the sandbox review.)
9. The extension's signature carries no Hardened Runtime exception entitlement (`com.apple.security.cs.*`) and no `get-task-allow`; `verify.sh` refuses to ship otherwise. macOS refuses to load a system extension with runtime exceptions (ref/toolchain T18).
10. No WireGuard UAPI *get* output (which contains `private_key`/`preshared_key`) leaves the extension or reaches a Swift `String`; stats use `wgGetStats` (§7.7, ref/wireguard D8). *Draft 8:* fork patch W11 removes `wgGetConfig`/`wgSetConfig`, so no UAPI get export exists at all, and `check-symbols.sh` pins the export count (§9.2).
11. A Release binary contains no Apple Development requirement clause (OID `1.2.840.113635.100.6.2.1`) and no `debugInjectFault` symbol (§5.3, §15.2).
12. *2.0.2:* the validator service's entitlements are exactly `{com.apple.security.app-sandbox}` (golden file, `verify.sh`); it links no AppKit, SwiftUI, Sparkle or NetworkExtension; the extension links no ZIPFoundation and the app no openvpn3 (§2.2, §2.4).

---

## 2. Xcode project, packages, signing

**Decision:** the native app lives in this repo under `native/` until cutover (§13), so history and the issue tracker stay in one place. CI jobs are path-filtered.

- `Packages/WireGuardBridge` from draft 3 is dropped: SPM forbids target paths outside the package root, so the vendored checkout itself is the package (ref/wireguard D16).
- **Synchronized folders (draft 8, Conflicts bd; PF 27).** xcodebuild 27.1 ignores a **folder** entry in `membershipExceptions`; only per-file entries exclude. **Rule: no non-target file under `App/`, `Tunnel/` or (2.0.2) `Validator/`.** Test packages and tools live under `Tests/` and `Tools/`. `verify.sh static` is to assert that the app and extension bundles contain no `.py`, test or `Screenshots` files, and the build is to fail if `App/UI/Tests` or `App/UI/Tools` exist (*draft 8: decided, not built yet*; neither directory exists today).
- **Fork repository (draft 8, Conflicts az; PF 18).** `github.com/steiale/wireguard-apple` doesn't exist yet. `vendor.sh` fetches the pinned upstream, applies the committed patch series, runs the bridge's Go tests and hash-checks every input, on every run (it no longer skips when `.git` directories exist). Creating the fork repository later changes nothing in the build.

### 2.2 Targets and SPM packages
